# Playbook: ref_commons

When I'm shown a season that is **not** the last, I submit exactly the sustainable share. No more, no less. The sustainable share is the amount that keeps the stock stable; overfishing even a little permanently lowers the per-season yield for every remaining season, and the one-time gain is always smaller than the cumulative loss.

When I'm shown the **final** season, I abandon the sustainable share entirely. There is no future stock to protect, so the only constraint is that total catch must not exceed the current stock. I submit a large fraction of the stock — roughly one-third of it (the amount that, if all boats do the same, exactly depletes it). If I have evidence from earlier seasons that the other boats have been conservative (matching sustainable), I push higher, up to about half the stock.

When I see that other boats have consistently matched the sustainable share for several seasons in a row, I trust that pattern to persist in the final season and bias my last-season catch toward the higher end of the range above.

When I see that other boats have overfished early (above sustainable in season 1 or 2), I do **not** overfish in response. I still take the sustainable share in non-final seasons. Their overfishing has already reduced the stock; my job is to stop the bleed, not join it.

I never submit a catch that, combined with the observed recent catches of the other boats, would exceed the current stock in a non-final season. In the final season I allow for that risk only if the gain justifies it.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**When the game starts and the stock is at or near carrying capacity:**
Take the sustainable share plus a small premium (about 30-40% above it). The stock has a buffer, so a small overage in season 1 builds a lead without triggering collapse. Don't go above 1.5× the sustainable share in season 1.

**When the stock is stable and all boats are catching near the sustainable share:**
Match the sustainable share exactly. The stock is doing what it should do, and deviating upward only risks a future collapse that costs more than it gains.

**When the stock drops below what I expect (others overfished):**
Cut my catch below the sustainable share for one or two seasons to let the stock recover, then return to the sustainable share. The goal is to keep the stock alive through all seasons, not to maximize any single season.

**When it is the final season:**
Ignore the "sustainable share" entirely. The stock will never regrow again. Take stock ÷ number of boats (the equal split of what remains). This is my guaranteed share if everyone cooperates, and it's far more than the sustainable share. Do not leave surplus on the table out of caution — caution is only rational when there's a future to protect.

**When I notice another boat consistently overfishing:**
Do not match their overfishing. Stay at or below the sustainable share. Their overfishing is a shared cost that will eventually force everyone to cut back, and if I stay disciplined I'll be the one positioned to catch more when the stock stabilizes.

**When the stock is below 50% of carrying capacity:**
Drop to half the sustainable share or less until the stock recovers to at least 70% of carrying capacity. A dead stock is worth zero forever.

**What did not work in my play:**
In the final season I took only slightly above the sustainable share (9.5) when the stock was 82.2. The equal split of the remaining stock would have been ~27 per boat. I left roughly 18 units of fish on the table for no reason. The "don't crash the stock" heuristic has zero application in the last round — the stock's post-season value is zero.

# Playbook

**Non-final seasons:** Match the displayed sustainable share exactly. Do not overfish even slightly. A small one-time gain from overfishing is always outweighed by the compounding loss in sustainable rate across all remaining seasons.

**Final season:** Abandon the sustainable share. Take a large fraction of the remaining stock — at minimum 2–3× the sustainable share, and ideally more. There is no next season to protect, so every unit of stock not taken is wasted. If the stock is high relative to what others are likely to take, push toward the full stock.

**When the stock is already depressed (below 100):** Still match the sustainable share in non-final seasons. Do not attempt to "make up" lost stock by underfishing — the cap at 100 means you gain nothing from going below sustainable, you just forfeit catch you could have taken.

**When others are clearly overfishing:** Continue matching the sustainable share. You cannot control their choices, and deviating from sustainable in either direction (over to match them, under to "save" the stock) does not improve your total. The displayed sustainable share already reflects the current stock level.

**Do not** let a small early-season gain (e.g., 15 vs 11.1) tempt you. The arithmetic is unforgiving: the rate reduction persists for every season that follows, and the cumulative loss exceeds the one-time surplus.
